title: Service Safeguard Architecture notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an alternative framing for graceful service continuity across regions and capacity tiers — a set of pragmatic controls and control-plane signals we can iterate on for Q1/2 2026. It is aimed at platform engineers, SREs, and product owners who need deterministic behavior for model routing when capacity or latency SLOs are threatened.

Scope and constraints:
- Apply to hosted + dedicated lanes; private deployments may adopt subset of controls where customers allow.
- Focused on request-level routing (not offline batch).
- Primary goals: keep high-priority traffic within latency SLOs, avoid cascading overload across regions, and preserve best-effort throughput for low-priority workloads.
- Assumes model catalog exposes 3 canonical variants per family: large/quality (Q), mid/quantized (M), small/distilled (S).

High-level strategy (conceptual):
1) Make routing decisions using an explicit "safeguard ladder": priority class -> model variant -> regional affinity -> fallback region. This ladder is used at request admission time and can be dynamically re-weighted by the control plane.
2) Prefer model-variant downgrades over outright rejection when latency or capacity is constrained (switchover thresholds are tunable per-customer/route).
3) Limit cross-region spill by applying a regional budget and soft-quotas; only overflow when local backpressure exceeds a configured threshold and global capacity can absorb.
4) Use circuit-breakers at two levels: per-model-variant and per-region. These are tripped based on tail latency, error rate, and queue depth.

Priority classes and desired behavior:
- Premium (SLA-backed): Never cross-region unless explicit failover; allowed to use M variant if Q is overloaded but only for short windows (e.g., 90s).
- Standard (paid): Prefer Q in-region, permit cross-region overflow after local circuit-breaker trips and only to regions within latency budget.
- Best-effort (free tier / background): Aggressive model trimming (prefer S/M), subject to immediate backpressure shed if global utilization > 85%.

Model variant mapping and hedging rules:
- Q (quality): baseline generation model (float/16 or bfloat). Target latency: 50-300ms depending on model. Managed with reserved capacity pools.
- M (mid): quantized or compilation-optimized variant. Used when Q latency degrades; target token quality ~95% of Q.
- S (small): distilled or small family; target for non-critical paths or when global demand spikes.
- Hedging policy: if request waits > t_hedge (configurable per route) and model invocation hasn't started, a hedged M or S call may be issued in parallel depending on priority class. Hedge ratio and concurrency capped to avoid double-charge or thrash.

Control plane signals and APIs (exposed internally):
- set_region_weight(region, route, weight) — used by autoscaler or SRE during incidents.
- trip_circuit(resource_id, reason, ttl) — used by monitoring automation.
- query_capacity(route, region) -> {available_gpus, reserved_slots, est_queue_ms}.
- suggest_variant(route, latency_ms, priority) -> recommended variant.
These are evented and surfaced to the routing layer via an internal pub/sub with versioned snapshots to keep decisions idempotent.

Regional overflow budgeting (to avoid thundering cross-region):
- Each region has an "overflow budget" per customer and per route (expressed in QPS or GPU-seconds per hour).
- Budget replenishment is time-windowed and visible in dashboards; crossing budget requires approval or automatic escalation to SRE.
- Overflow decision matrix: only permit overflow if: local_queue_ms > Q_local_threshold AND target_region.latency_est <= route.latency_budget AND overflow_budget_remaining > 0.

Autoscaling and reserved pools interplay:
- Reserved pools (dedicated) are the first line: always route to reserved if available for the customer's priority class.
- Autoscaler reacts to queue_ms and token throughput; scaling cooldowns are tuned to prevent oscillation when downgrades are active.
- Warm-up: when initiating region-to-region overflow, prefer spinning up M variants first (cheaper) before Q instances; if Q instances are needed, escalate.

Observability and SLOs to drive decisions:
- Key signals: p95/p99 latency per model-variant, per-region queue_ms, token throughput, model error ratios, GPU utilization by pool, overflow_budget usage.
- Alerts: automatic trip when p99 > 2x target for > 60s (per-route); this triggers a control-plane policy change (reduce region_weight or switch default variant).
- Dashboards: per-customer route view with variant mix, regional split, and a short-run projection of overflow budget.

Runbook sketch (incident where region R1 is overloaded):
1) Monitoring detects p99(R1, Q) > thresh -> auto trip Q variant circuit for R1 (ttl 90s).
2) Routing control plane reduces weight for R1.Q and increases weight to R1.M and R2.Q by configured fractions subject to overflow budget.
3) If R1.M also degrades -> enable cross-region overflow to R2 & R3 for Standard traffic; Premium remains pinned to in-region but moved to M.
4) If global capacity is insufficient -> start shedding best-effort traffic and throttle new Standard on-ramps.
5) Post-incident: run quality regressions on sampled outputs, notify product owners if variant switches lasted > 10 minutes.

Canary and rollout considerations:
- When altering default variant mapping or overflow budgets, release via small percentage rollouts (1%, 5%, 25%) and monitor divergence in generation quality and latency.
- Maintain a prompt-based evaluation set to detect quality regressions when automatically switching to M or S.

Configuration examples (pseudo-yaml):
route: /v1/generate/newsletter
  priority: standard
  variant_preference: [Q, M, S]
  local_overflow_threshold_ms: 300
  overflow_budget_per_hour: 5000 # GPU-seconds
  hedging: {enabled: true, t_hedge_ms: 120}

Open questions / trade-offs to decide:
- Default hedging strategy: parallel vs sequential fallback (cost vs latency).
- How aggressive should overflow be for mixed latency-sensitive routes (embedding vs generation)?
- Tenant isolation: should overflow budgets be global per-tenant or per-route?
- Billing/observability: how to surface cross-region execution for cost audits?

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype: implement an internal control-plane flag that can flip variant preference for a single high-traffic route (owner: Daniel Kwon, JIRA-PE-618). Target: POC by 2026-01-30.
- Dashboard: add overflow_budget widget to infra dashboard and a run-rate projection. (owner: Aisha Martinez)
- Runbook authoring: convert this draft into an incident playbook with checklist steps and Slack automation hooks. (owner: Priya Raman)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on cross-region overflow to prioritize latency and cost predictability. Suggest we test more aggressive overflow in non-customer-impacting routes first.
- Keep comments inline — I expect several iteration rounds as autoscaling knobs land.

-- end --
